extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory; playwrights and creative writers studying tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing and evaluating tragic drama in the Aristotelian tradition, focusing on plot, character, emotion (pity/fear), katharsis, and the dramatic unities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero: moral likeness combined with elevated station (ὅμοιος)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic sufferer is 'a man like ourselves (ὅμοιος)'; the resemblance is one of moral character. The hero 'rises above the common level in moral elevation and dignity, but he is not free from frailties and imperfections.' He should be 'a prince or famous man who falls from a height of greatness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a character with 'rich and full humanity' — elements other men possess but more harmoniously or potently blended. The hero must be sufficiently like us so we can identify and merge our sympathy with him, yet raised in external dignity to provide an ideal distance and grandeur. Avoid making the hero either flawless/perfect or a consummate villain; also avoid purely parochial or bourgeois figures incapable of universalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear must be combined
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's requirement: tragedy should evoke both pity (ἔλεος) and fear (φόβος). 'The requirement of Aristotle is pity and fear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to awaken both emotions in close alliance; some plays may predominately evoke one, but the full tragic effect (and the katharsis) depends on their union. Be aware that inferior tragedies may excite only one of the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of tragic fear (imaginative, impersonal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic fear is 'not the crushing apprehension of personal disaster' nor merely fear of a future event; it is an imaginative, almost impersonal emotion arising from close identification with the hero, a 'shudder of horror or of vague foreboding' and a thrill of awe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray fear as arising from sympathetic identification (we feel 'liable to suffering' ourselves) and from the sense of moral inevitableness, not as narrow selfish terror. Avoid treating tragic fear as mere imminent physical danger or as simple future-based dread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katharsis: purification/purgation of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic katharsis involves the expulsion or purification of the painful element in pity and fear by artistic treatment, so that the emotions are 'so transformed that the net result is a noble emotional satisfaction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure emotion so that the selfish, egoistic elements are removed or universalised by the artifice of the play; the spectator should be lifted beyond individual self-regard into a purified pleasurable calm. This is the aesthetic end rather than a direct moral improvement, though indirect moral effects may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalisation / representation of the universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy represents the universal: 'The characters it depicts, the actions and fortunes of the persons with whom it acquaints us, possess a typical and universal value.' Artistic unity should reveal 'the law of human destiny' so incidents become images of larger human issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subject-matter and incidents that can be enlarged into typical, universal meanings rather than merely private, accidental, or sentimental events. The play should enable spectators to read broader human law or destiny in particular events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (organic unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requirement is unity of action: an organic unity in which the whole is complete (τέλειον), its parts arranged in fixed order (τάξις), and the successive incidents connected by an inward causal bond (necessary and probable sequence). 'None can be removed, none transposed, without disturbing the organism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a single, complete action (πρᾶξις) where incidents follow by causal or probabilistic necessity; avoid epeisodic plots that are mere sequences of striking scenes without inward connexion. Ensure every scene/part is necessary to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude (μέγεθος)
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain magnitude is indispensable: the whole must be of such size that the memory or mind's eye can embrace and retain it. Objects either infinitely large or infinitesimally small are unfit for artistic representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the scale suitable to allow full, harmonious evolution of the plot — not so vast (e.g., the entire Trojan War) that it fragments into disconnected scenes, nor so trivial that it cannot sustain tragic development. Allow sufficient length for natural development but avoid undue prolixity or irrelevant material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-defined beginning, middle, and end (causal sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end.' A beginning does not itself follow anything by causal necessity; an end naturally follows something else and has nothing following it; the middle follows something and is followed by something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate point of commencement that does not force infinite retrospection; ensure the plot's causal chain is neither arbitrarily extended backward nor left open-ended. The middle must causally connect beginning and end; avoid beginnings that import necessary precedents or endings that do not conclude the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denouement must arise from the plot itself (no deus ex machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: The λύσις (Dénouement) must 'arise out of the plot itself,' and not be brought about by accident or by a Deus ex Machina. Resolutions should be the inevitable, though perhaps unexpected, consequences of what has gone before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid resolving the action by arbitrary devices, accidents, or external contrivances; the catastrophe or solution should feel like the natural outcome of the established causal chain. The anecdote about the 'fifth act' warns against resolutions that betray the preceding acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις) and Reversal (περιπέτεια) integrated into the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex (πεπλεγμένη) plots the catastrophe is often worked out by surprises of Recognition and Reversal; these 'surprises' must be woven into the tissue of the plot and discovered to be 'the inevitable, though unexpected, consequences of all that has preceded.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognition and reversal to intensify tragic emotions, but ensure they emerge organically from the plot's causal structure (not as contrivances). Surprises should be both unforeseen and demonstrably necessary in retrospect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter based on permanent/objective realities; avoid narrow egoistic motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions suitable for katharsis 'must have their basis in the permanent and objective realities of life, and be independent of individual caprice or sentiment.' 'The more exclusive and self-absorbed a passion is, the more does it resist kathartic treatment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer themes rooted in broad social, moral, or existential realities rather than purely private or sentimental motives (e.g., narrow love stories are rarely tragic unless tied to larger issues). Avoid parochial or squalid motives that limit the spectator's ability to be lifted above the individual case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic (ἐπεισοδιώδης) structure and artless scene-sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle condemns 'epeisodic' plots where scenes follow one another 'without the inward connexion of the εἰκός or ἀναγκαῖον.' A succession of stirring scenes does not constitute a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute a series of striking situations, rapid contrasts, or isolated pathetic effects for an internally connected plot. Ensure each episode is causally integrated into the whole and contributes to the tragic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reference to outward/accidental conditions of stage representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle rejects as inartistic any reference to the outward and accidental conditions of stage representation (e.g., appeals to the mechanics of performance or contests) when considering the length and structure of a play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the play's structure according to artistic and psychological laws (unity, magnitude, causal development), not the contingent practicalities or spectacle-related considerations. Keep structural choices grounded in aesthetic principles rather than extraneous stage-conditions.
